topics.description: The JDK compiles Java source into bytecode; the runtime executes it.
learningGoals: A clean checkout builds with a documented JDK
A failing test causes the build to fail
examples: A coupon project builds on a fresh checkout.

material.explanation: The JDK compiles Java source into bytecode; the runtime executes it. A repeatable build must compile and run tests outside your IDE. Choose Maven or Gradle and use its wrapper.

workedExample.scenario: A coupon project builds on a fresh checkout.
steps: Record the JDK version.
Run the wrapper to compile and test.

commonMistakes: An IDE run configuration is not a reproducible build.
guidedExercise: Run one passing and one failing test from the terminal
material.independentExercise: Document how another person can build the project without your IDE.
recallQuestions: What does the compiler produce?
Why commit the build wrapper?

acceptanceCriteria: A clean checkout builds with a documented JDK
A failing test causes the build to fail

topics.title: Values, references, and null

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Java passes arguments by value.
learningGoals: Mutation and reassignment predictions match execution
Required null inputs are rejected explicitly
examples: Two variables reference one GiftCard.

material.explanation: Java passes arguments by value. For an object, the copied value is a reference: two variables can reach the same mutable object. Null represents no object and must be handled at explicit boundaries.

workedExample.scenario: Two variables reference one GiftCard.
steps: Spending through either reference changes the same card.
Reassigning a method parameter does not reassign the caller's variable.

commonMistakes: Java does not pass objects by reference.
material.independentExercise: Write examples distinguishing equal strings, identical references, and absent values.
recallQuestions: What is copied into a method parameter?
Why can two variables observe the same mutation?

acceptanceCriteria: Mutation and reassignment predictions match execution
Required null inputs are rejected explicitly

topics.title: Classes and objects
topics.description: A class defines an object's state and behavior; each instance has its own identity.
learningGoals: Two instances retain independent state
Behavior changes only the intended instance
examples: Create two cards with balances 50 and 20.

tasks.title: Explain Classes and objects in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A class defines an object's state and behavior; each instance has its own identity. Instance fields belong to an object, while static fields are shared. Put state-changing rules behind behavior methods.

workedExample.scenario: Create two cards with balances 50 and 20.
steps: Spend 10 from the first.
Their balances become 40 and 20.

commonMistakes: A static balance would accidentally share money across cards.
material.independentExercise: Model a coupon with a code, expiration, and remaining uses.
recallQuestions: What belongs to the class rather than an instance?
Why is a card more than a bag of fields?

acceptanceCriteria: Two instances retain independent state
Behavior changes only the intended instance

topics.title: Constructors
topics.description: A constructor establishes a valid starting state.
learningGoals: Invalid construction cannot produce an object
Valid boundary values are tested
examples: Construct a 150-percent coupon.

tasks.title: Explain Constructors in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A constructor establishes a valid starting state. Reject missing or impossible values immediately rather than requiring callers to repair an object after creation. Constructor validation does not replace validation of later mutations.

workedExample.scenario: Construct a 150-percent coupon.
steps: Reject the discount before storing state.
A valid 10-percent coupon starts usable.

commonMistakes: Setters after construction cannot guarantee an object was always valid.
guidedExercise: Reject blank code and invalid discount
material.independentExercise: Construct a GiftCard that rejects negative opening balances.
recallQuestions: Which rules belong at construction?
Which rules must also be checked later?

acceptanceCriteria: Invalid construction cannot produce an object
Valid boundary values are tested

topics.title: Encapsulation
topics.description: Encapsulation keeps an object's invariants under its own control.
learningGoals: All public mutation paths enforce invariants
Callers cannot mutate internal collections
examples: A card holds 20.

tasks.title: Explain Encapsulation in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Encapsulation keeps an object's invariants under its own control. A private field with an unrestricted setter still exposes the rule. Prefer meaningful operations and avoid returning mutable internal collections.

workedExample.scenario: A card holds 20.
steps: spend(25) rejects without changing balance.
spend(5) leaves 15.

commonMistakes: Private fields alone do not make a design encapsulated.
material.independentExercise: Expose coupon activation and redemption without public state setters.
recallQuestions: How can a getter break encapsulation?
Who guarantees a nonnegative balance?

acceptanceCriteria: All public mutation paths enforce invariants
Callers cannot mutate internal collections

topics.title: Interfaces
topics.description: An interface describes operations callers rely on.
learningGoals: The caller uses only the contract
Implementations obey the same behavioral expectations
examples: A service depends on a TokenHasher contract.

tasks.title: Explain Interfaces in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: An interface describes operations callers rely on. Implementations must preserve the same meaning of success and failure. Introduce a contract for a real boundary, not automatically for every class.

workedExample.scenario: A service depends on a TokenHasher contract.
steps: A fake records calls in a test.
The production implementation preserves matching semantics.

commonMistakes: An interface with no useful boundary only adds indirection.
material.independentExercise: Define a notification boundary and two small implementations with consistent behavior.
recallQuestions: What does the caller need to know?
What must every implementation preserve?

acceptanceCriteria: The caller uses only the contract
Implementations obey the same behavioral expectations

topics.title: Enums
topics.description: Enums represent named values from a finite set.
learningGoals: Unknown states cannot enter the model
Illegal transitions preserve the previous state
examples: A card is ACTIVE, BLOCKED, or EXPIRED.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Enums represent named values from a finite set. They prevent arbitrary strings but do not enforce transitions by themselves. Keep legal transitions in domain behavior rather than scattered string comparisons.

workedExample.scenario: A card is ACTIVE, BLOCKED, or EXPIRED.
steps: Blocking changes ACTIVE to BLOCKED.
Spending while BLOCKED is rejected.

commonMistakes: An enum does not automatically make every state change legal.
guidedExercise: Replace status strings with an enum
material.independentExercise: Model order status while rejecting repeated cancellation.
recallQuestions: What does an enum prevent?
Where do transition rules belong?

acceptanceCriteria: Unknown states cannot enter the model
Illegal transitions preserve the previous state

topics.title: Records
topics.description: Records provide a concise representation of fixed components with generated accessors and equality.
learningGoals: Record values remain stable after caller mutation
Equality behavior is demonstrated
examples: A receipt record contains line items.

tasks.title: Explain Records in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Records provide a concise representation of fixed components with generated accessors and equality. Their component references are final, but referenced objects can still mutate. Copy mutable inputs when the record promises stable values.

workedExample.scenario: A receipt record contains line items.
steps: Copy the input list at construction.
Later changes to the caller's list do not alter the receipt.

commonMistakes: A record containing a mutable list is not automatically deeply immutable.
guidedExercise: Attempt to mutate its input list
material.independentExercise: Model a token issuance result without exposing mutable secret buffers.
recallQuestions: What does final protect?
When does a record need defensive copying?

acceptanceCriteria: Record values remain stable after caller mutation
Equality behavior is demonstrated

topics.title: Exceptions
topics.description: Exceptions signal that normal completion did not occur.
learningGoals: Failures are distinguishable by category
Rejected operations leave state unchanged
examples: A card holds 10 and spend(15) fails.

tasks.title: Explain Exceptions in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Exceptions signal that normal completion did not occur. Distinguish invalid input, rejected business operations, and infrastructure failures. Preserve useful causes and ensure a rejected operation does not partially mutate state.

workedExample.scenario: A card holds 10 and spend(15) fails.
steps: Throw a meaningful failure.
Verify the balance is still 10.

commonMistakes: Catching Exception and continuing can hide an invalid state.
guidedExercise: Inspect the failure type and message
material.independentExercise: Separate a missing token from an unavailable token store in your design.
recallQuestions: Which failures should callers handle?
What must remain unchanged after rejection?

acceptanceCriteria: Failures are distinguishable by category
Rejected operations leave state unchanged

topics.title: Collections
topics.description: Collection choices follow required operations: sequence, unique membership, or keyed lookup.
learningGoals: Each choice follows explicit access requirements
Ordering and duplicate behavior are tested
examples: A service needs users by ID and ordered audit events.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Collection choices follow required operations: sequence, unique membership, or keyed lookup. Program against an appropriate contract while understanding implementation costs, mutation, iteration, and null policies.

workedExample.scenario: A service needs users by ID and ordered audit events.
steps: Choose Map for ID lookup.
Choose List for event order.

commonMistakes: Choosing by familiarity ignores ordering and duplicate requirements.
guidedExercise: State required operations before choosing a collection
material.independentExercise: Choose structures for active sessions and revoked token IDs with reasons.
recallQuestions: Which contract preserves duplicates?
What operation makes a map useful?

acceptanceCriteria: Each choice follows explicit access requirements
Ordering and duplicate behavior are tested

topics.title: List
topics.description: A List represents an ordered sequence and may contain duplicates.
learningGoals: Order and duplicates are preserved
Empty and invalid-index behavior is explicit
examples: Events are login, refresh, refresh.

tasks.title: Explain List in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A List represents an ordered sequence and may contain duplicates. Indexes describe positions, not permanent identity. Removing elements shifts later positions, so business identifiers should not depend on list indexes.

workedExample.scenario: Events are login, refresh, refresh.
steps: All three remain in order.
Removing index zero moves later positions.

commonMistakes: A list index is not a stable database-style identifier.
material.independentExercise: Implement an ordered session-event history and test empty access.
recallQuestions: Does a List imply unique values?
Why should an entity ID differ from its index?

acceptanceCriteria: Order and duplicates are preserved
Empty and invalid-index behavior is explicit

topics.title: Set
topics.description: A Set expresses unique membership using its equality rules.
learningGoals: Repeated IDs do not increase size
Retention and ordering assumptions are documented
examples: Add request ID R1 twice.

tasks.title: Explain Set in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A Set expresses unique membership using its equality rules. Iteration order depends on the implementation. Uniqueness applies to the chosen key: two requests with different IDs can still represent the same business operation.

workedExample.scenario: Add request ID R1 twice.
steps: The second insertion reports existing membership.
The set still contains one ID.

commonMistakes: A set alone does not define a business idempotency policy.
material.independentExercise: Track revoked token IDs and define when entries can be removed.
recallQuestions: What makes two values duplicates?
How does unbounded membership affect memory?

acceptanceCriteria: Repeated IDs do not increase size
Retention and ordering assumptions are documented

topics.title: Map
topics.description: A Map associates each unique key with a value.
learningGoals: Missing lookup is handled safely
Duplicate-key behavior is deliberate
examples: Store session S1 for user U1.

tasks.title: Explain Map in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A Map associates each unique key with a value. Inserting an existing key can replace its value. Decide whether missing keys and null values are allowed, and never assume a lookup succeeded before using its result.

workedExample.scenario: Store session S1 for user U1.
steps: Replace S1 with an updated session.
Looking up S2 reports absence.

commonMistakes: A key can map to null in some implementations, so null need not prove absence.
guidedExercise: Test insert, replace, and missing lookup
material.independentExercise: Build a user-by-ID index with explicit duplicate-ID behavior.
recallQuestions: What happens when a key is inserted twice?
How do you represent an absent value?

acceptanceCriteria: Missing lookup is handled safely
Duplicate-key behavior is deliberate

topics.title: Optional
topics.description: Optional expresses that a returned value may be absent.
learningGoals: Both present and absent cases are covered
Absence does not become an accidental exception
examples: A repository lookup returns no token.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Optional expresses that a returned value may be absent. It encourages deliberate handling but does not replace all null validation or every field type. Avoid blindly calling get and distinguish cheap defaults from expensive fallback work.

workedExample.scenario: A repository lookup returns no token.
steps: The caller maps absence to a rejection.
No token behavior is invoked.

commonMistakes: Optional.get without a presence decision just moves the failure.
material.independentExercise: Write a coupon lookup that does not expose null to its caller.
recallQuestions: What does Optional communicate?
When does a fallback expression execute?

acceptanceCriteria: Both present and absent cases are covered
Absence does not become an accidental exception

topics.title: Instant
topics.description: Instant identifies a point on the timeline independent of local display conventions.
learningGoals: Validity uses timeline values
The exact expiration boundary is tested
examples: Issued at 10:00Z, a token expires at 10:15Z.

tasks.title: Explain Instant in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Instant identifies a point on the timeline independent of local display conventions. Compare instants for token expiration, and choose whether equality with expiresAt is already expired. Keep human time zones separate from validity rules.

workedExample.scenario: Issued at 10:00Z, a token expires at 10:15Z.
steps: 10:14:59Z is valid.
10:15:00Z is expired under the chosen rule.

commonMistakes: A local date-time without a zone is not an unambiguous instant.
material.independentExercise: Display the same expiration in two zones while keeping identical validity.
recallQuestions: What changes when a time zone changes?
Is equality with expiresAt valid in your policy?

acceptanceCriteria: Validity uses timeline values
The exact expiration boundary is tested

topics.title: Duration
topics.description: Duration represents an amount of elapsed time rather than a calendar date.
learningGoals: Time units are explicit
Invalid zero or negative lifetimes are rejected
examples: A reset lifetime is 15 minutes.

tasks.title: Explain Duration in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Duration represents an amount of elapsed time rather than a calendar date. Express lifetimes with explicit units and distinguish a duration from an instant. Calendar days across clock changes need different reasoning from fixed elapsed hours.

workedExample.scenario: A reset lifetime is 15 minutes.
steps: Add it to issuedAt.
The result is an expiration instant, not another duration.

commonMistakes: A duration is not a timestamp or a local calendar day.
material.independentExercise: Make token lifetime configurable through a validated Duration.
recallQuestions: What is produced by adding Duration to Instant?
Why can a calendar day differ from 24 hours?

acceptanceCriteria: Time units are explicit
Invalid zero or negative lifetimes are rejected

topics.title: Clock injection

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Obtain current time through an injected Clock when behavior depends on time.
learningGoals: No expiration test relies on sleeping
Production and test clocks use the same behavior path
examples: A test fixes the clock at expiresAt.

material.explanation: Obtain current time through an injected Clock when behavior depends on time. Production can use a real clock while tests use fixed instants. This removes sleeps and makes expiration tests repeatable.

workedExample.scenario: A test fixes the clock at expiresAt.
steps: The service reads the injected clock.
The token is rejected without waiting.

commonMistakes: Sleeping in a test is slow and can still miss the intended boundary.
guidedExercise: Replace direct now calls with a clock
Use two fixed clocks around expiration
material.independentExercise: Test coupon expiration at three exact instants without sleeps.

What makes a fixed-clock test deterministic?

acceptanceCriteria: No expiration test relies on sleeping
Production and test clocks use the same behavior path

topics.title: Immutability
topics.description: Immutable objects cannot change their observable value after creation.
learningGoals: Inputs cannot alter the value after construction
Returned values cannot mutate internals
examples: A receipt copies its items.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Immutable objects cannot change their observable value after creation. They reduce aliasing surprises and make value reasoning easier. Domain entities may still need controlled mutation; do not confuse immutability with a ban on useful behavior.

workedExample.scenario: A receipt copies its items.
steps: A caller edits the original list.
The receipt's observable content remains unchanged.

commonMistakes: Final references do not prevent mutation of referenced objects.
material.independentExercise: Create an immutable Money value and compare it with a mutable account entity.
recallQuestions: What does observable immutability mean?
Which domain state genuinely needs to change?

acceptanceCriteria: Inputs cannot alter the value after construction
Returned values cannot mutate internals

topics.title: equals
topics.description: equals defines logical equality and must behave consistently as an equivalence relation.
learningGoals: Equality laws pass focused tests
The identity or value decision is documented
examples: Two CouponCode values contain SAVE10.

tasks.title: Explain equals in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: equals defines logical equality and must behave consistently as an equivalence relation. Decide whether objects represent identity or values before implementing it. Equality used in collections must agree with hashCode.

workedExample.scenario: Two CouponCode values contain SAVE10.
steps: They compare equal even as different objects.
Their hashes must also match.

commonMistakes: Reference identity and logical equality answer different questions.
guidedExercise: Compare null and a different type
material.independentExercise: Define equality for a session identifier without mutable status fields.
recallQuestions: What makes two entities the same entity?
Why does equality need transitivity?

acceptanceCriteria: Equality laws pass focused tests
The identity or value decision is documented

topics.title: hashCode
topics.description: A hash narrows lookup candidates; equality decides whether keys match.
learningGoals: Equal values have equal hashes
Collisions preserve correct lookup behavior
examples: Insert a key whose hash uses mutable status.

tasks.title: Explain hashCode in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A hash narrows lookup candidates; equality decides whether keys match. Equal objects must have equal hashes, but unequal objects may collide. Fields used by hash-based keys must remain stable while the key is stored.

workedExample.scenario: Insert a key whose hash uses mutable status.
steps: Change status.
Lookup may fail because it searches a different bucket.

commonMistakes: A hash is not an object's memory address or a unique identifier.
guidedExercise: Replace the key with a stable value
material.independentExercise: Test custom session keys with deliberate collisions.
recallQuestions: Can different objects share a hash?
Why can mutation break lookup?

acceptanceCriteria: Equal values have equal hashes
Collisions preserve correct lookup behavior

topics.title: Generics
topics.description: Generics describe type-safe operations without erasing useful caller information at compile time.
learningGoals: The example compiles without unchecked casts
Read and write constraints are explained
examples: List<GiftCard> is not List<Object>.

tasks.title: Explain Generics in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Generics describe type-safe operations without erasing useful caller information at compile time. Invariance prevents unsafe writes through a widened collection type. Bounds and wildcards express which values may be read or written.

workedExample.scenario: List<GiftCard> is not List<Object>.
steps: Adding a String through the latter would corrupt the promise.
A read-only wildcard can express a narrower need.

commonMistakes: A generic type does not make arbitrary runtime casts safe.
material.independentExercise: Write a helper that reads a collection of entities without adding incompatible values.
recallQuestions: Why are generic collections invariant?
What does an upper bound permit?

acceptanceCriteria: The example compiles without unchecked casts
Read and write constraints are explained

exercises.title: Coupon
exercises.description: Model a coupon whose valid state and redemption rules cannot be bypassed.
learningGoals: Model a coupon whose valid state and redemption rules cannot be bypassed.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: An active 10-percent coupon has two uses and expires at noon.

tasks.title: Coupon code
Percentage discount
Expiration
Maximum usage count
Activation state
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Invalid codes, discounts, and use limits cannot construct a coupon
Verify: Inactive, expired, and exhausted coupons reject redemption without mutation
Verify: Exactly one use is consumed per successful redemption
Verify: Money rounding and expiration boundaries have tests

requirements: Nonblank code; percentage discount from 1 through 100
Positive maximum uses and explicit active state
Expiration supplied as Instant; expired when now is at or after expiresAt
Redemption requires active, unexpired, unused capacity
A rejected redemption does not consume a use
Compute a monetary discount under a stated rounding policy
constraints: Plain Java; no Spring or database
Use an in-memory implementation and a repeatable build
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: Use Coupon to practice constructor validation, controlled mutation, time, and decimal arithmetic together. Keep the coupon responsible for its own usability rules. Choose whether codes are normalized and document that policy; do not silently change identity.

workedExample.scenario: An active 10-percent coupon has two uses and expires at noon.
steps: One successful redemption consumes one use.
At noon another redemption is rejected without consuming the remaining use.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Use an injected Clock to test before, at, and after expiration.
Test the final available use and every rejection state.
material.independentExercise: Add activation and deactivation, then prove callers cannot bypass the same redemption rules.
recallQuestions: Which object owns remaining uses?
Where and how is discount rounding applied?

acceptanceCriteria: Invalid codes, discounts, and use limits cannot construct a coupon
Inactive, expired, and exhausted coupons reject redemption without mutation
Exactly one use is consumed per successful redemption
Money rounding and expiration boundaries have tests
